49106: How to read the Bible faithfully: noticing our assumptions, reading by genre and context, telling stories from commands, letting Scripture interpret Scripture, and holding the Bible's paradoxes together. Each lesson gives tools to avoid common misreadings and to read with Jesus at the centre.
49108: When the Bible tells a story, is it telling me what to do? How do I know which parts are commands for me and which are simply a record of what happened?
49109: Much of the Bible describes what people did without approving it. A story records; a command instructs. If we treat the whole Bible as a rule book, we end up copying what God never asked us to copy.
49110: Two kinds of text: record and instruction
49111:
A descriptive text tells us what happened. A prescriptive text tells us what we should do. Both are inspired and both teach us, but they teach in different ways. Genesis tells us that Jacob married two sisters and their two servants. Leviticus and Deuteronomy give Israel laws. The first is a record; the second is an instruction.

About 40 percent of the Old Testament is narrative, and Acts and the Gospels are largely narrative too. Bible narratives are usually told without much comment. The writer shows us the events and expects us to see the results. That is why so many readers have taken a story as a command: they assumed that if it is in the Bible, God must approve of it.

Being in the Bible means God wanted us to know it happened. It does not mean God wanted it to happen. Paul says the stories of Israel were written as examples and warnings for us. Some examples are to follow; many are warnings.
49113:
Polygamy. Lamech, Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had more than one wife. The text never commands it, and the stories show the damage: rivalry between Sarah and Hagar, between Leah and Rachel, and Solomon's wives turning his heart away. Deuteronomy warns kings not to multiply wives, and Jesus goes back to the creation pattern of one man and one woman.

Jephthah's vow. Jephthah promised to sacrifice whatever came out of his house, and it was his daughter. The narrator does not praise him. God had already forbidden child sacrifice, and the book of Judges is built to show a nation falling apart, ending with the refrain that everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

Lot's daughters made their father drunk and conceived by him. The story explains the origins of Moab and Ammon; nobody has ever read it as a model. Gideon's fleece is similar but more subtle: Gideon had already received God's word, and his double test shows a frightened man asking for reassurance. God was patient with him, but the text does not present the fleece as a method for finding God's will.
49114: The harder cases: Acts and the early church
49115:
Acts is the hardest book for this question, because it tells the story of the church we belong to. In Acts 1 the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias. Is that how churches should choose leaders? Most readers say no: the lot was an accepted Jewish way to seek God's decision, it happened before Pentecost, and we never see it again in the New Testament. Later, leaders are chosen through prayer, the community and the Spirit's guidance.

In Acts 2 and 4 the believers shared their goods and sold property for anyone in need. Some groups have read this as a command for all Christians to hold everything in common. But Peter tells Ananias that the land was his own and the money was under his control; the sin was lying, not keeping. The sharing was voluntary and generous. The principle (care for the poor in the family of faith) is commanded again and again; the exact form is described.

The Pentecostal tradition raises a fair question here: Luke is a theologian too, and he tells stories in order to teach. Roger Stronstad and others argue that Luke's pattern of Spirit-empowerment is meant to be normative. So the question is not 'Does narrative ever teach?' (it does) but 'What exactly is this narrative teaching, and how do we know?'
49117:
Some texts really are commands, but the form they take is tied to a culture. Paul says five times, 'Greet one another with a holy kiss.' Jesus says, 'You also ought to wash one another's feet.' Paul tells women in Corinth to cover their heads when they pray or prophesy.

Most churches keep the principle and change the form: warm, pure welcome (a handshake or an embrace), humble service to one another, and honour in public worship. Others keep the form as well. Some Mennonite, Amish and Brethren churches keep head coverings; Seventh-day Adventists, many Brethren and some Baptists wash feet as an ordinance; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches wash feet on Maundy Thursday. These are sincere choices, not mistakes.

How do we tell the principle from the form? We look at the reason given. When a command is grounded in God's character, the gospel or creation, it tends to carry over unchanged. When it is grounded in custom ('Does not nature itself teach you…?', 'we have no such practice'), it is more likely to be cultural. Even then, careful readers disagree about 1 Corinthians 11, because Paul appeals to both creation and custom.
49118: If we see the Bible as a rule book, it goes wrong
49119:
The learner who asked for this course put it simply: if we see the Bible as a rule book, it goes wrong. History proves the point. Polygamy has been defended from the patriarchs. Slavery was defended from the household codes and from Israel's laws. Holy war and violence against neighbours were justified from the conquest stories. In each case people found a text, removed it from its story and turned it into a rule.

The Bible is first a story: God creating, calling a people, rescuing, warning, and finally coming in Jesus. Laws and commands live inside that story. Israel's laws were given to a particular people at a particular time, and the New Testament says some of them were a shadow of what was to come. Jesus himself said some laws were given 'because of your hardness of heart'.

This does not mean the Bible has no commands. It is full of them: love God, love your neighbour, forgive, make disciples, do this in remembrance of me. It means we read every command in the light of the whole story and of the One the story leads to. A rule-book reading asks only 'Is there a verse for it?' A story reading asks 'Where does this fit, and what does it show us about God?'
49121: Sort each passage. Is it a story that records what happened, a command whose principle binds us while its form may change, or a command that applies to Christians directly? Then read why. Some answers are debated; the notes say so.
49122: Descriptive: a record, not a command
49123: Command: keep the principle, form may change
49125: Jacob marries Leah and Rachel and has children by their servants too.
49127: Never commanded. The story shows the rivalry and pain it caused. Jesus points back to one man and one woman.
49128: Jephthah vows to sacrifice whatever comes out of his door first.
49129: A rash vow in a book about Israel's moral collapse. God had forbidden child sacrifice (Deut 12:31).
49130: Gideon puts out a fleece to test God's word twice.
49131: Gideon already had God's word. The story shows God's patience with a fearful man, not a method for guidance.
49132: The apostles cast lots to choose Matthias.
49133: A recognised Jewish practice, used before Pentecost and never again in the New Testament. Most traditions do not treat it as a rule.
49134: The believers had all things in common and sold possessions to meet needs.
49135: Voluntary generosity (Acts 5:4). The principle of caring for the poor is commanded elsewhere (Gal 2:10, 1 John 3:17); the exact form is described, not required.
49136: Lot's daughters get their father drunk and conceive by him.
49137: An origin story for Moab and Ammon, told without approval. No one has read it as a pattern to follow.
49138: Ananias and Sapphira fall dead after lying about their gift.
49139: A unique event at the church's founding. It teaches that God takes honesty seriously; it is not a promise that liars in church will die.
49140: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
49142: A real command, repeated five times. Most churches keep the principle (warm, pure welcome) in a local form.
49143: A woman should cover her head when she prays or prophesies.
49144: Debated. Many read the covering as a local sign of honour; some churches keep it as binding because Paul also appeals to creation (1 Cor 11:8-9).
49145: You also ought to wash one another's feet.
49146: Debated in form. All agree on humble service; some churches keep foot-washing as an ordinance, others on Maundy Thursday only.
49147: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.
49149: Jesus' own teaching to his disciples, grounded in the character of the Father (Matt 5:45). It applies without translation.
49150: Commanded by Jesus and practised by the church from the beginning. Traditions differ on its meaning, not on whether to do it.
49151: Is this a command for me?
49152: A simple tree for any passage. It will not settle every debate, but it will stop most of the common mistakes.
49154: What kind of text is it?
49155: A story: it tells what someone did
49156: An instruction: it tells someone what to do
49157: Does the narrator, or a later passage, comment on what happened?
49158: It is condemned or shown to cause harm
49159: It is praised and also taught plainly elsewhere
49161: Who was the instruction given to?
49165: How does the New Testament treat this law?
49167: It says Christ fulfilled or ended it
49169: What reason does the text give for the command?
49170: God's character, the gospel or creation
49173: Does your reading of it fit the way Jesus lived and taught: love for God and neighbour?
49174: It seems to work against love
49176: The story shows what happens when people go their own way. Learn from it; do not copy it.
49177: A good example backed by teaching
49178: The story illustrates something the Bible also commands. Follow the teaching; the story gives it colour.
49180: The text records what happened. Ask what it shows about God and people, but do not turn it into a rule.
49181: For that person, with a lesson for us
49182: Paul asking for his cloak is not a command for you. Look for the wider truth, if there is one.
49183: Sacrifices, food laws and similar laws point to Christ. Learn what they meant and how Jesus completes them.
49184: Keep the principle, translate the form
49185: Find the reason behind the command and ask how that reason is best honoured where you live.
49187: This applies to Christians today. Obey it with love and with the help of the Spirit.
49189: Sincere Christians disagree here. Study the context, listen to other traditions and hold your conclusion humbly.
49190: Rule book or story? Two ways of holding the Bible
49193: A manual of instructions and precedents
49194: A true story of God and his people, with commands inside it
49196: Is there a verse for it?
49197: Where does this passage sit in the story, and who was it for?
49200: Records that often warn rather than model
49202: Rules to apply directly (or quietly ignore when awkward)
49203: Gifts to Israel, read through Christ who fulfils them
49204: Takes the words seriously and wants to obey
49205: Takes the words seriously and asks what they meant then
49206: Has defended polygamy, slavery and violence
49207: Can be used to explain away commands we dislike
49208: Narrative teaches only what is taught elsewhere
49209: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart (How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth); much evangelical teaching
49210: A story is normative only when the writer clearly intends it to be, which is usually shown when the same point is taught plainly elsewhere. Otherwise narratives illustrate; they do not command. This is the most widely taught rule in evangelical hermeneutics.
49211: Simple, testable and protective. It stops people building practices on single events such as Gideon's fleece or casting lots.
49212: Pentecostal and narrative scholars say it underrates Luke and the Old Testament writers as theologians who teach through stories. It can make narrative feel second-class.
49214: Roger Stronstad (The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke); many Pentecostal scholars
49215: Luke-Acts is history written to teach. Repeated patterns, such as believers being filled with the Spirit and empowered to witness, are intended as a model for the church in every age.
49216: Takes the purpose of biblical narrators seriously and explains why Luke tells similar stories several times.
49217: Critics ask which patterns are normative: Acts also shows lots, shared property and different orders of baptism and the Spirit (Acts 2:38, Acts 8:14-17, Acts 10:44-48). Choosing among them needs a principle outside the story.
49219: The Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement (Churches of Christ), many Brethren and some Anabaptist groups
49220: The church should follow the patterns of the apostolic church in Acts and the letters as closely as possible: in worship, leadership, baptism and church life. Examples in Scripture can function as commands.
49221: A sincere desire to obey and not to add human traditions. It has kept practices such as weekly communion and simple worship.
49222: Different restoration groups reach different patterns from the same texts, which shows that selection and interpretation are still at work.
49224: William J. Webb (Slaves, Women and Homosexuals); related ideas in N. T. Wright's 'five-act play' model
49225: Some commands moved their culture forward but not all the way. We should follow the direction the text was moving (for example, toward the dignity of slaves) rather than freeze its first form.
49226: Explains why the church rightly rejected slavery even though Scripture regulated rather than abolished it.
49227: Conservatives such as Wayne Grudem argue it lets readers decide which direction is 'redemptive'. Progressives sometimes say it does not go far enough.
49229: Christocentric readers such as Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak and Brian Zahnd; the learner's own position
49230: Jesus is the key. He showed which laws were concessions to hardness of heart and which reveal the Father. Any reading that makes God unlike Jesus has misread the passage. The question 'Is it Christlike?' sorts the rule-book problem at the root.
49231: Matches Jesus' own way of handling the law (Matt 5 and Matt 19:8) and guards against using Scripture to justify violence.
49232: Others ask who defines 'Christlike', and point out that Jesus himself affirmed the law and spoke of judgement. Lesson 14 looks at this in detail.
49233: 'Putting out a fleece' to find God's will
49234: When you face a decision, ask God for a sign. If the sign happens, the answer is yes. Gideon did this and God answered.
49235: Gideon had already been told clearly what to do (Judg 6:14-16) and had already received a sign (Judg 6:21). The fleece shows his fear, not his faith; he even apologises for asking (Judg 6:39). The book of Judges presents Gideon as a flawed leader whose story ends in idolatry (Judg 8:27). Scholars such as Daniel Block and Barry Webb read the fleece as a sign of weak trust that God graciously tolerated.
49236: Many careful evangelicals agree. Some add that God can and does guide through circumstances, and that a humble prayer for confirmation is not sinful. The issue is turning a story into a method that replaces Scripture, wisdom and community.
49237: Fleece-guidance can turn decisions into superstition and make people think God failed them when a sign does not come.
49238: Acts 2 as a command to abolish private property
49239: Some readers say Acts 2:44-45 shows God's ideal economy and that all Christians should hold everything in common. Others, reacting, say the passage has nothing to say to us at all.
49240: The sharing was voluntary (Acts 5:4) and practical, aimed at needs in a community where many had come from abroad and some had lost family support. It echoes the promise that there should be no poor among God's people (Deut 15:4). Luke presents it as the fruit of the Spirit, not a law. Scholars such as Craig Keener and Luke Timothy Johnson note its links to ancient ideals of friendship ('friends hold all things in common').
49241: Traditional scholars agree it is descriptive in form but insist it is not irrelevant: radical generosity is commanded throughout the New Testament (2 Cor 8:13-15, 1 John 3:17). The story inspires; the commands bind.
49242: One mistake turns generosity into compulsion; the other turns a beautiful picture of the Spirit's work into a museum piece.

49252: Hermeneutics: how to read the Bible
49254: Scripture Interprets Scripture (and the One-Verse Problem)
49255: How do I let the whole Bible explain its hard parts? Why is it dangerous to build a teaching on one verse or one event? And is 'Is it biblical?' really the right question to ask?
49256: The Bible is one story with one centre. Clear passages shed light on unclear ones, the whole shapes the parts, and the whole points to Jesus. A doctrine built on a single verse, read alone, is standing on one leg.
49258:
The Reformers called it the analogia scripturae, the 'analogy of Scripture'. The idea is old. Augustine taught that the plainer passages should be used to throw light on the more obscure ones. The Westminster Confession (1646) says the infallible rule for interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself: when the meaning of one passage is unclear, we search other places that speak more clearly.

This works because the Bible, for all its many authors over roughly 1,500 years, tells one connected story. A word, an image or a promise in one book is picked up and developed in another. The lamb in Exodus, the suffering servant in Isaiah and the Lamb in Revelation explain one another.

Jesus himself did this. When the devil quoted Psalm 91 to tempt him to jump from the temple, Jesus did not deny the psalm. He answered, 'It is also written,' and quoted Deuteronomy. One verse, pulled out alone, was being used against the purpose of the whole.
49260:
The learner who asked for this course wrote: 'There is a huge problem in building teachings and theologies around one event or one scripture.' Church history agrees. Here are some examples.

Mark 16:18 says believers 'will pick up serpents'. In the early 1900s some Pentecostals in Appalachia, following George Went Hensley, began handling venomous snakes in worship. People have died, and the practice continues in a few small churches. Yet Mark 16:9-20 is missing from the two oldest complete Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus), and even if it is accepted, the only biblical example (Paul and the viper on Malta) is an accident survived, not a test staged.

1 Corinthians 15:29 mentions people 'baptised for the dead'. It is the only verse on the subject, and scholars have proposed dozens of explanations. The Latter-day Saints built a large practice of proxy baptism on it. Most Christian scholars think Paul is referring to a local practice to make a point about resurrection, without approving it. Matthew 16:28 ('some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming') has been used to argue that all prophecy, including Christ's return, was fulfilled by AD 70; others read it of the transfiguration that immediately follows, or of the resurrection and Pentecost.

Other single texts carry heavy loads too. Acts 5 (Ananias and Sapphira) has been used to frighten believers into giving or into silence before leaders. 1 Timothy 2:15 ('saved through childbearing') has been read as if women are saved by having babies; scholars read it in several other ways, all agreeing it cannot contradict salvation by grace. Malachi 3:10 has been used to promise financial blessing in return for tithing to a local church, though it was addressed to post-exilic Judah about supporting the Levites through the temple storehouse.
49261: How to let the Bible explain itself
49262:
First, read the whole passage and the whole book before you decide what a verse means. Second, ask whether the verse is clear or unclear, central or marginal. A teaching repeated across many books by many writers (that God is love, that Christ died and rose, that we are saved by grace) carries more weight than an obscure phrase mentioned once.

Third, let the clear explain the unclear, not the other way round. If one strange verse seems to contradict the main teaching of the Bible, the problem is probably with our reading of the strange verse. Fourth, notice where different writers emphasise different things. Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works; James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Read together, they correct each other's misuse: Paul against earning, James against empty belief.

Finally, remember that Scripture interpreting Scripture does not mean flattening every book into one voice. Comparing passages should help us hear each writer better, not force them all to say the same thing.
49264:
The learner adds a further point: the question 'Is it biblical?' is the wrong first question, and 'Is it Christological?' (that is, does it fit Christ?) is the right one. The reasoning is this. Almost anything can be called 'biblical' if you find the right verse: slavery, polygamy, holy war and snake handling all had their verses. Religion, the learner says, tries to prove an issue just because it is written, and does not check whether it fits the nature of God.

This view has deep roots. Martin Luther judged the books of Scripture by whether they 'promote Christ'. Hebrews says God spoke in many ways through the prophets but finally in his Son, the exact imprint of his nature; John says Jesus has 'exegeted' the Father. Jesus told the scholars of his day that they searched the Scriptures but would not come to him, though the Scriptures testified about him. In this reading, the Bible is the witness and Jesus is the Word it witnesses to. Bill Johnson's phrase 'Jesus is perfect theology' and Tommy Miller's 'Jesus is the measure that measures all' express the same conviction.

The critiques deserve an equal hearing. Who defines 'Christlike'? Our picture of Jesus comes from the Bible, so we cannot set Jesus against the Bible without risk of shaping a Jesus we prefer. Jesus also spoke of Gehenna more than anyone else in the New Testament, drove traders from the temple, pronounced woes on religious leaders and will judge the world. A 'Christlike' test that leaves those out is not testing by the real Christ. And the early church rejected Marcion, who set the God of Jesus against the God of the Old Testament. Many therefore suggest both questions belong together: 'Is it biblical?' read as 'Does it fit the whole Bible's witness?', and 'Is it Christlike?' read as 'Does it fit the whole Christ the Bible shows?'
